title: Second Normal Form: Partial Dependencies
description: With a composite key, any attribute that depends on only part of that key is sitting in the wrong table. EnrolmentSheet has three such attributes — and the one most people miss depends on two of the three key columns rather than one. Why it matters: 2NF is the form that surrogate keys hide rather than fix.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

`EnrolmentSheet` is keyed on `(StudentId, CourseCode, Term)` — the three things that together identify one enrolment. The repeating groups are gone, so the table is in first normal form.

It is still wrong, and now the wrongness has a precise shape.

> **Second normal form:** no non-key attribute depends on only *part* of a composite key.

The practical test is a question you ask of every non-key column:

> **"If only part of the key changed, would this column change with it?"**
>
> Or, more usefully: **"which part of the key do I actually need in order to know this value?"**

If the answer is "less than the whole key", the column is in the wrong table.

## Scenario

```sql
SELECT * FROM EnrolmentSheet ORDER BY StudentId, CourseCode;
```

Work through the columns one at a time.

### 1. `StudentName`, `StudentEmail` — depend on `StudentId` alone

Thandi's name does not change when she enrols in a different course. You need only `StudentId` to know it. So it depends on **one third of the key**, and it is stored once per enrolment — which is precisely the update anomaly from module 11, still unfixed.

### 2. `RoomBuilding`, `RoomCapacity`, `InstructorOffice`… wait

Hold these. They are a different problem, and module 14 deals with them. Note them and move on — part of the skill here is not fixing everything at once.

### 3. `InstructorName`, `RoomCode` — depend on `(CourseCode, Term)`

**This is the one people miss.** It is easy to check each key column on its own, decide `InstructorName` depends on neither `CourseCode` alone nor `Term` alone, and conclude it must depend on the whole key.

It does not. Run this:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT CourseCode, Term, InstructorName, RoomCode FROM EnrolmentSheet;
```

Two rows, for four enrolments. Everyone taking `DB101` in `2026S1` has Dr Naidoo and room R101 — the instructor and the room are facts about **the course in that term**, and `StudentId` has nothing to do with them.

A partial dependency does not have to be on a *single* key column. It is any **proper subset** of the key, and `(CourseCode, Term)` is a proper subset of `(StudentId, CourseCode, Term)`. Two out of three still counts.

### 4. `Grade` — depends on the whole key

Thandi got an A in `DB101` and a B in `ST200`. Change any one of the three key columns and the grade changes. `Grade` is the only column that genuinely belongs on this table.

## Your task

Give each dependency the table its determinant keys:

- **`Student (StudentId, StudentName, StudentEmail)`**, keyed on `StudentId`.
- **`CourseOffering (CourseCode, Term, InstructorName, InstructorOffice, RoomCode, RoomBuilding, RoomCapacity)`**, keyed on **`(CourseCode, Term)`**.
- Drop all seven moved columns from `EnrolmentSheet`, leaving `(StudentId, CourseCode, Term, Grade)`.
- Add a foreign key from `EnrolmentSheet.StudentId` to `Student`.

Carry `InstructorOffice`, `RoomBuilding` and `RoomCapacity` across to `CourseOffering` for now, unchanged. They do not belong there either — but their problem is a different one, and putting them there first is what makes module 14's point visible.

## Why the instructor goes on the offering, not the course

This is a modelling decision, not a mechanical consequence, and it is worth stating out loud.

You could put `InstructorName` on `Course`. It would look tidier — one fewer column on the offering. But it asserts something false: **that a course has one instructor, forever.** Dr Naidoo teaches `DB101` in `2026S1`; next year it may be someone else, and next semester it may be two people.

Who teaches a course is a fact about **the course in a term**, which is exactly `CourseOffering`'s key. Putting it on `Course` would be the same class of error you have been removing all along — attaching a fact to the wrong thing.

Remember this decision. **Module 15 depends on it**, and it will not work if the instructor is on `Course`.

## What to look for

**2NF only bites on composite keys.** If a table's primary key is a single column, no proper subset of it exists to depend on, so the table is in 2NF automatically. This sounds like good news and is a trap: giving `EnrolmentSheet` an `EnrolmentId IDENTITY` surrogate key would make it 2NF-compliant **without moving a single column**. The redundancy would be exactly where it was; it just would no longer be visible in the key.

This is the honest case against reflexive surrogate keys. They are often right — module 4 argues for them — but a surrogate key does not fix a dependency problem, it **hides** it. If you use one, work out the natural key anyway and keep it as a `UNIQUE` constraint; that is where the dependencies stay legible.

**`EnrolmentSheet` still carries a foreign key to `Course`, and there is now a sharper option.** With `CourseOffering` in place, `(CourseCode, Term)` on an enrolment could reference the *offering* rather than the course — which would also stop anyone enrolling in a term the course was never offered in. That is a genuine improvement and not what this module grades; notice it, and notice that decomposition keeps creating new places for constraints to live.

**What decomposition bought here.** `Student` now has one row per student, so an email can no longer disagree with itself — the update anomaly from module 11 is finally dead. `CourseOffering` can record that `DB301` runs in `2026S2` in room R110 before anyone signs up.

## How this is graded

Structurally, as always: `Student` exists and is keyed on `StudentId`; `CourseOffering` exists and is keyed on `(CourseCode, Term)`; `InstructorName` and `RoomCode` are on the offering; the moved columns are gone from `EnrolmentSheet`; the foreign key to `Student` is there.

The grader **cannot see functional dependencies.** Nothing in `sys.columns` records that `StudentId → StudentEmail`; that is a fact about students, not about the schema. What the check verifies is the structural fingerprint that a correct 2NF decomposition leaves behind — not the reasoning that should have produced it.

steps.prompt: Run SELECT DISTINCT CourseCode, Term, InstructorName, RoomCode FROM EnrolmentSheet — four enrolments collapse to two rows, which is the partial dependency made visible.
Model Student keyed on StudentId and CourseOffering keyed on (CourseCode, Term), move the seven columns across, and link EnrolmentSheet to Student.

hints: Take each non-key column and ask which part of the key you need to know its value. StudentName needs only StudentId. Grade needs all three.
A partial dependency can be on more than one column — (CourseCode, Term) is a proper subset of the key, so InstructorName and RoomCode are partial dependencies too. This is the one that gets missed.
CourseOffering's primary key is both CourseCode and Term together. Keying it on CourseCode alone would say a course runs in exactly one term, which is not true.
Copy the rows across with SELECT DISTINCT before dropping the columns — and expect CourseOffering to end up with two rows from four enrolments.
